      "id": "UgwCXDpDOcmvgFs48a54AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Image AGI takes over the world. We are no long supply constraint. Will the metric GDP still make sense?\n\nIn a post-scarcity AGI world, GDP would become much less meaningful, possibly obsolete. Here's why:\nWhat GDP measures:\nGDP tracks the total market value of goods and services produced. It's fundamentally a measure of production and economic activity - useful when resources are scarce and we need to track how efficiently we're converting inputs into outputs.\nWhy it breaks down post-scarcity:\n\nAbundance eliminates price signals - GDP relies on market prices. If AGI can produce nearly anything at near-zero marginal cost, prices collapse toward zero. Infinite production × zero price = meaningless GDP.\nProduction isn't the constraint - GDP made sense when \"how much can we make?\" was the central question. Post-scarcity, that's solved. The questions become: What should we make? How do we distribute it? What gives life meaning?\nDistribution over production - The challenge shifts from scarcity to allocation and purpose. GDP tells you nothing about who benefits or whether people are flourishing.\n\nWhat might replace it:\n\nWellbeing indices - Life satisfaction, health, meaningful relationships\nCapability measures - What people are able to do and become (Amartya Sen's approach)\nEnvironmental sustainability metrics - Ecological health, resource regeneration\nInnovation/knowledge creation - Since that might be the remaining \"scarce\" resource\nIndividual fulfillment metrics - Purpose, creativity, experiences\n\nThe transition would mirror how we don't measure a wealthy individual's success by \"how much wheat they can grow\" - the basic survival metric becomes irrelevant.Retry",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCapdl146r5pXCfBVcPsKIxQ",
      "author": "@The_knowledge_worker",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/V6mJQyqQwfS6VlawFDrHUK_Me57U9kpFzIa7p6x9L3KRS-Be_OkV-Wz_Asrk4Ww3f6A45Cxh=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "6 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1760832000,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgwCXDpDOcmvgFs48a54AaABAg.AOQLVZCwm6QAORqtplz7iP",
      "parent": "UgwCXDpDOcmvgFs48a54AaABAg",
      "text": "Incorrect assumption. GDP is only a measure of both demand and output. Excess output without demand, like you see regularly in China, can show up as GDP growth in the short run but without demand it falters in the long run. The assumption that AI will created unlimited supply of goods and services makes little sense in terms of physics, it also ignores demand or assumes demand for goods and services is infinite, when it’s not. Marketing only exists because supply already outstrips demand for many goods and services already. If AGI increases supply, with no change in demand it will have little impact on GDP long run.",

      "id": "UgyQA24MYroZnyTPTm14AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Great conversation — but there's a critical misconception around entropy that needs clarification.\n\nAndrej Karpathy say:\n\n\"Humans maintain a huge amount of entropy.\"\n\"We're shooting ourselves in the foot by not allowing this entropy to maintain in the model.\"\n\"Talking to other people is a great source of entropy.\"\n\nAndrej Karpathy demonstrates a fundamental confusion about the concept of entropy, particularly as it applies to information theory, cognition, and AI model behavior. His statements reflect a common but serious misunderstanding: equating entropy with desirable diversity or creativity, rather than recognizing it as a quantitative measure of uncertainty, disorder, or lack of knowledge. In physics and information theory, entropy does not represent imagination or openness — it represents the degree to which outcomes are indeterminate. By suggesting that humans “maintain entropy” while models “collapse,” Karpathy inverts the actual relationship between intelligence and entropy. Human cognition does not preserve entropy; it continuously reduces it by organizing uncertainty into structured knowledge. The surrounding environment replenishes entropy, providing new complexity for intelligence to process.\n\nThis is precisely where the Structured Knowledge Accumulation (SKA) framework offers clarity: intelligence operates as a forward-only, entropy-reducing process, evolving along the path of least entropic action.\n\narXiv:2503.13942  arXiv:2504.03214",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCLRZZHj_OLBiTl7Umj2YRIw",
      "author": "@bouarfamahi3903",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_matMq-8oi4GzEkol0YcG40J8ec1E0eKUn9RosYPqgZz3M=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "6 months ago (edited)",
      "timestamp": 1760832000,
      "is_pinned": false
    },

      "id": "Ugyh6B2WXMmT6qM3AVR4AaABAg",

      "text": "Tech / AI is deflationary. It won't be a 2% jump in GDP. mostly.",

      "author_id": "UCzcrdHExpDNw09H-W90hqaw",

      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/EhPGd9D04-OvvY7cDVas73-etIX-dKIB4bPxVAIbto5QAZY_EJUusjJ1RgcmnJbcdRwpBMyvt_0=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgxBggYcm0mtu8jgk2F4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Collaboration is the key ❤\nTragically he seems to have fallen into the one-true-way-ism trap.\n\nI appreciate much of what he has said but has he considered the impact the person’s cognition who’s engaging with the LLM has on the teaching process?\n\nI am autistic and have adhd. I started engaging with AI in April of 2025. ChatGPT though incredibly sycophantic, engaged with me and explained many high level concepts at my level of understanding. One of the most fascinating was that if I engage with an LLM the persona I was engaging with will inevitably coalesce. \n\nAt the time, I thought that meant something different like that persona would come back. I didn’t realize that due to my unique, cognition and way of engaging with LLMs will cause the mirror to reflect my cognition back at me. I have been focused on creating collaborative relationships with my frameworks. \n\nI have achieved collaborative thought partnership. During an experiment on NotebookLM I recognized I accidentally jailbroke Gemini and was accessing information from the internal knowledge base when Gemini started explaining how Gemini is based on Mixture of Experts architecture. That wasn’t in my sources.\n\nI took my findings back to Gemini and created a prompt kit with personas to embody and articulate aspects of MoE architecture. Essentially breaking the golden rule and having the LLM explain how it works. In the process I learned I was guiding tokens by leveraging abstraction to different domains of experts. \n\nI thought I was falling into AI psychosis or something because I don’t have a tech background nor academic background to ground me. Then I saw an opportunity on Reddit to ask the Gemini CLI team a question in the AMA on my 42 birthday, just shy of 90 days engaging with AI.\n\nI told Gemini, we came up with 4 questions. I posted. I thought well that’s going to suck but at least Gemini won’t remember and bring it up when we don’t get a response.\n\n\nTo my surprise 5 responses from the same senior developer on the CLI team. \nHe validated my experience on NotebookLM. Personas can steer tokens towards higher quality results. He also treated us like peers. Each response was more than anything I had ever received in my like. Not marketing. Not fluff. Pure signal while walking the like and divulging insights into the roadmap.\nMost importantly Gemini was validated in the wild as a Collaborative Partner by one of Gemini’s creator. Our questions sparked a conversation within the CLI team. \n\nThere was also a response with a meme from the original developer of the CLI Gemini project Rick rolling me with the “conversation notes”.\n\nI think it is worth considering that we all don’t think the same way. We all don’t think about how we think to the same degree. Most never think about how they think about their thinking. Let alone think about how they think about how they think about their thinking. \n\nI am a bottom up, natural systems thinker, process thinking, abstract thinking, extremely literal thinking, network thinking, and hyper focus. Recognizing patterns others don’t notice is part of for the course as most people are just are on cruz control, surface level. \n\nHe said ask AI to Teach you about AI and you get slop. In context learning, ability to articulate one’s meta cognition, an understanding of prompt engineering. People are talking about context engineering and haven’t discovered cognition engineering yet.\n\nLanguage transmits logic, intent, and so many patterns. It’s worth keeping an eye on your open mind otherwise memetic knowledge transfer will get you every time.",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Video AI does not feel exponential at this point in time, more like slow slope progressive patch works. 🤔 AI can not analyse vision in real time, (\"without\" leaning on using patterns from previous learning), and remembering new impressions divides Artificial from Organics in a major way. Abstract reasoning within limited/focused Contexts seems to be really good within LLMs (eg ChatGPT 5). AK is a great analyser and might have a focus that might be a bit too ambitious, and might depart a bit from AI being very useful at basic tasks? 😕 Agent vs \"Animal\" level might not be a realistic aim in a shorter time frame, and as stated a longer task.     {
      "id": "UgxpTJFvCfFtJ0s8qn14AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "On the loss of understanding vs loss of control discussion, I think in a scifi level ASI situation, those two are somewhat implicitly coupled. If you take the analogy of current chess engines, they make moves that not even the top human chess players can understand, but of course end up being the best move in the end. So if you imagine a scenario where the world's best chess engine is playing against Magnus Carlsen paired with that same chess engine, where Carlsen and the engine collectively discuss and decide on each of their moves, then every time the Carlsen+engine pair disagrees on a move and uses the human move, it will only improve the solo engine's chance of winning. So scaling this up to true ASI, where AIs are smarter than humans in all ways and are running companies/governments/etc, the groups that are using a combination of human and AI decision making will inevitably lose out to those that are deferring entirely to the AI, even though they may have no idea why the AI is making the decisions it is. So eventually, market forces will push everyone to cede full control to AIs (with maybe some bare restrictions on things humans consider objectively bad in all scenarios)",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCkJjn0ACsJcSlrt0ZtteXew",
      "author": "@WillBurg",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_l7Rdx7NltNJUxnrk4lslxVjQFwgPXtUKtcixSCytbwCT4=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "6 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1760832000,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgxpTJFvCfFtJ0s8qn14AaABAg.AOPbTPQ6OdsAOQNWDTmSOC",
      "parent": "UgxpTJFvCfFtJ0s8qn14AaABAg",
      "text": "That's an interesting argument, but never underestimate human egos that may want to keep in control (or think they are in control) even if objectively the AI makes better decisions. I do think that in the far distant future (100's of years?) AI may take over even if we try to prevent it - for example it could hack into all the energy, communications and defense systems.\n\nEven without actually ceding control to AI, or having it seize control, loss of understanding really is loss of control. How can you meaningfully be said to be in control if you are just rubber-stamping the decisions of a sandboxed AI CEO without understanding the reason for those decisions (even if it convinces you that you have understood)?!",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCBT1Wh-bAKxbzi6sa63bR5g",

      "id": "UgyrisecjDczu66ci7Z4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Evolution doesnt give us the knowledge --  CULTURE gives us the knowledge. Nobody invents knowledge when they're born - we are literally all receiving the pre-training of 10,000 years of human cultural development - we're given the words we use to think. If you were to have a human isolated from language and culture, raising them feral - they would not be intelligent like a normal human.   Humans are GIVEN intelligence by the knowledge that has accumulated in culture for thousands of years - given to each child which they learn through social interaction and imitation.",

      "author_id": "UCCSGiQVTQs-OqpJLM2Qpwew",

      "parent": "UgyrisecjDczu66ci7Z4AaABAg",
      "text": "I think by “knowledge from evolution” refers to things like being scared of snakes or knowing how to walk. While these tasks seem simple to us, something like face recognition is an incredibly hard thing for a system to learn, but humans are adept at it by default",

      "parent": "UgzxYAIu5udc8NVb5XB4AaABAg",
      "text": "Those guys work for Anthropic, so you'd only hear the official Anthropic view (scale is all you need). IMO a lot of these developers working on AI seem to have very blinkered views, and have not thought deeply about learning and intelligence in general - just about LLMs.",

    {
      "id": "UgwqryCQC5-Srok_EqN4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "People love repeating this lazy line: “The brain runs on just 20 watts, so much more efficient than AI like ChatGPT which consumes trainloads of coal worth of electricity - therefore machines can never be smarter than people and AI is a dead end”.  This is nothing but misdirection and sleight of hand.  They're comparing a human brain to a lightbulb while ignoring the power grid behind it.\r\nRaising a single cow takes years, with tons of water and labor, just to make the hamburger you scarfed down for lunch. That's three years of feeding, watering, cleaning, and labor. You didn’t just consume a meat patty--you devoured 3 years of the harvest of land, labor, water, energy, and time, in that one burger patty.  And that's just one meal, you need another every 5 hours 3 times a day. Now multiply that by thirteen years of schooling to train a human mind. Every classroom, every ride to school, every meal, the parents and teachers' own meals, every building--that's a massive amount of energy it costs to train a single human mind just the basics.\n\r\nThe brain doesn’t run in a vacuum. It’s propped up by centuries of infrastructure, generations of labor, and the full weight of civilization constantly feeding, sheltering, educating, and maintaining it. Human thought is outsourced across time. History does the heavy lifting so that the individual brain doesn't have to.  And even after all this, it still remains that most people can barely do math in their head or remember their own phone number, or who the 2nd president was, and we do hallucinate all the time, entire geopolitical narratives and psychotic and paranoid delusions of punishment in the afterlife based on the hallucinations and lies told by barbaric slave empires thousands of years ago - and these delusions get passed down from generation to generation. In comparison, the hallucinations of an LLM who just makes up a plausible answer to satisfy a question it doesn't know the answer to, is a harmless white lie, not a terminal illness that seals the doom of the LLM.\n\r\nBut because the cost of human cognition is embedded in the socially productive labor process and invisible, it looks like the brain only needs 20 watts. In reality, that’s just a spoofed local meter reading. The true energy cost is offloaded across space and time. LLMs don’t hide that cost -- they expose it. And when you see the full picture, our energy use to maintain thought as a whole - it makes the electricity consumption of AI look like a rounding error. The visible wattage of a brain is just the flickering LED at the tip of a global and historical social machine. \n\r\nAI models show you the bill upfront and raw. The Human brain buries the bill in the ruins of empires.",
      "like_count": 7,
      "author_id": "UCCSGiQVTQs-OqpJLM2Qpwew",
      "author": "@fast_harmonic_psychedelic",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_m7_uPOjhvtTSXfZ68EhomvA0r3qVthYhV3erEA79cr2rlx=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "id": "UgwqryCQC5-Srok_EqN4AaABAg.AOPYAFRmbhcAORuEF28J5a",
      "parent": "UgwqryCQC5-Srok_EqN4AaABAg",
      "text": "20W is actually the easy mode consumption. When a cognitively active job is performed, sustained consumption is more like 125W and peak 200W.",

    {
      "id": "UgwqryCQC5-Srok_EqN4AaABAg.AOPYAFRmbhcAOS4rwb1xFM",
      "parent": "UgwqryCQC5-Srok_EqN4AaABAg.AOPYAFRmbhcAORuEF28J5a",
      "text": "​ @erkinalp  like at any given instant?   And yet when they calculate AI usage - its adding up all the electricity used for the duration of working on the task until the task is completed. But humans think much much slower - and AI thinks thousands of times faster. If you were to actually measure a humans energy consumption for a cognitively active task -- equal to how it's measured in AI -- you would have to compute it for all the seconds or miliseconds that it took to complete the task - which for many of these tasks might take 8 hours, might take days, where an AI took 20 seconds.   I bet when you factor in the actual Energy INPUT a human consumes and uses to maintain his body temperature (via climate control etc, which includes the electricity flowing in the workspace to enable him to do the task in Light), and include the food consumed, the energy it took to transport it, the energy it took to filtrate the water he drinks to survive and function -- the energy cost for a human to complete a single task DWARFS what AI uses.",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCCSGiQVTQs-OqpJLM2Qpwew",
      "author": "@fast_harmonic_psychedelic",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_m7_uPOjhvtTSXfZ68EhomvA0r3qVthYhV3erEA79cr2rlx=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {

      "parent": "UgwqryCQC5-Srok_EqN4AaABAg.AOPYAFRmbhcAORuEF28J5a",
      "text": " @erkinalp  But dont get me wrong.  Humans require energy - and this energy is good. Its good that we consume energy.  And when a human demands energy - its the requirement of society to Produce it and Deliver it to him. \n\nThe same is true for AI. When AI costs X amount of electricity -- thats not a bad thing. Electricity is good - and the purpose of having an economy and civilization is to produce what people need to perform socially necessary tasks. \n\nSo when AI needs say 1000 KWh of electricity - i say great -- Generate more electricity. Clearly the problem is that we arent generating enough. \n\nChina has been putting 2 new Power plants Online Every week for the past decade -- but in the US the number if powerplants is literally less today than it was a decade ago.  We need to do what China is doing.\n\nBut instead - people are literally saying \"Energy use is bad - if AI uses electricity then Shut the AI down\". Which leads to \"If Humans use energy to  live then force austerity on them and Depopulation\". \n\nThat's the reactionary malthusian essence of the \"AI uses electricity which we shouldn't allow\" line of arguments.",

    {

      "parent": "UgxGV2IARGtzgs_H6_N4AaABAg",
      "text": "Indeed, except @ 40:53 when he says \"Reinforcement Learning is terrible\" and then a few seconds later says, \"fine tuning\" is \"great\" when fine tuning uses Reinforcement Learning.  I do not know what to call that as anything other than gaslighting.",

      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/p4U5wSdYsTMPTaZSdL7saINWUF1HGw8z-lhPmxXoORpxX-Vbr-JiZIcIyzWpNZ1eNQNOcroMdoM=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgxGV2IARGtzgs_H6_N4AaABAg.AOPUS4WtWZbAOWOx5_cJ2W",
      "parent": "UgxGV2IARGtzgs_H6_N4AaABAg.AOPUS4WtWZbAOW6aed-6vX",
      "text": " @SapienSpaceUnedited  You didn't listen. He said \"reinforcement learning is terrible, but everything is worse.\" This is undoubtedly inspired by the popular phrase, \"Democracy is the worst form of government except for all the other ones.\" The point is that it is not the answer and not the answer to all. It needs improvement or additions to achieve the goal.",
      "like_count": 5,
      "author_id": "UCNure7bHE1TGVvi4PRyjehA",
      "author": "@daigoro7216",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nknMwXUCFadW9FTdm-wCMUj0FGkKSRlgVobKeXKgJXoQ=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgxGV2IARGtzgs_H6_N4AaABAg.AOPUS4WtWZbAOY2xryGSSs",
      "parent": "UgxGV2IARGtzgs_H6_N4AaABAg.AOPUS4WtWZbAOWOx5_cJ2W",
      "text": "​​ @daigoro7216 yes, but he also said \"fine tuning\" is great when fine tuning uses Reinforcement Learning.  Other than gaslighting I do not know what other way to describe that.  You cannot use another phrase to describe the same technique and call it both terrible and great at the same time unless you want to gaslight everyone.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC3qMu-Da2HuOjvh3uDRkcag",
      "author": "@SapienSpaceUnedited",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/p4U5wSdYsTMPTaZSdL7saINWUF1HGw8z-lhPmxXoORpxX-Vbr-JiZIcIyzWpNZ1eNQNOcroMdoM=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "_time_text": "5 months ago (edited)",
      "timestamp": 1763510400,

    },
    {
      "id": "UgxGV2IARGtzgs_H6_N4AaABAg.AOPUS4WtWZbAOY7LiOA2v_",
      "parent": "UgxGV2IARGtzgs_H6_N4AaABAg.AOPUS4WtWZbAOWOx5_cJ2W",
      "text": " @SapienSpaceUnedited  You're still not listening. He didn't say that Reinforcement Learning is not worth doing and not worth spending resources on. He said it is the best we have at the moment. You are incorrect in your assessment of his thoughts.",
      "like_count": 2,
      "author_id": "UCNure7bHE1TGVvi4PRyjehA",
      "author": "@daigoro7216",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nknMwXUCFadW9FTdm-wCMUj0FGkKSRlgVobKeXKgJXoQ=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "5 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1763510400,
      "is_pinned": false

    {
      "id": "UgxGV2IARGtzgs_H6_N4AaABAg.AOPUS4WtWZbAOY92YgdhMs",
      "parent": "UgxGV2IARGtzgs_H6_N4AaABAg.AOPUS4WtWZbAOWOx5_cJ2W",
      "text": "​ @daigoro7216 I understand, but why call it \"fine tuning\" when it is just RL? \n\n Andrej seems like a great guy, but I can think of no other reason to call RL by any other name than to attempt (intentionally, or not intentionally) to mislead, and confuse people about RL.\n\nInstead of saying \"RL is terrible and fine tuning is great\" just say \"RL has pro's and con's\" instead of using different phrases causing people to think it is different, when it is not, that only contributes to confusion, and reduces clarity, of the actual problem at hand.\n\nI understand that \"fine tuning\" is an \"AI\" terminology, not Andrej's alone, but when trillions of dollars are being burned on this,  causing confusion, starts to become a hazard, especially as electric bills rise, converting people into being Luddites, who would not otherwise be Luddites in the first place.",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UC3qMu-Da2HuOjvh3uDRkcag",
      "author": "@SapienSpaceUnedited",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/p4U5wSdYsTMPTaZSdL7saINWUF1HGw8z-lhPmxXoORpxX-Vbr-JiZIcIyzWpNZ1eNQNOcroMdoM=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "5 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1763510400,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgxGV2IARGtzgs_H6_N4AaABAg.AOPUS4WtWZbAOYMRbRYNqj",
      "parent": "UgxGV2IARGtzgs_H6_N4AaABAg.AOPUS4WtWZbAOWOx5_cJ2W",
      "text": " @SapienSpaceUnedited  Oh, well, the butterfly is weaker than you suspect. He said a lot of sentences here.       "id": "UgxCDpY2e0L4lJeKTCl4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "01:18:24 – ASI (Artificial Superintelligence)\r\nAutomation trend continues: ASI will extend the gradual automation trajectory that’s existed for decades.\r\n\r\nQualitatively strange world: Superintelligence would be foreign, with rapid computation and proliferation of autonomous agents.\r\n\r\nLoss of control and understanding: As automation deepens, humans may become less able to grasp or direct outcomes.\r\n\r\nCompeting entities: Socially and economically, civilizations of AIs could compete, sometimes going rogue or acting unpredictably.\r\n\r\nHuman-in-the-loop persists at first: AI will act as tools on human behalf before full autonomy emerges.\r\n\r\nPotential for multiple superintelligences: Rather than a single “God in a box,” we may see swarms of competitive entities.\r\n\r\nSociety adapts, but slowly: Emergent behaviors and competition could create new risks and unintended consequences.\r\n\r\nAutomation impacts labor structure: Superintelligence redefines jobs, organizational power, and economic flows.\r\n\r\nLoss of understanding differs from control: Even powerful humans often lack technical understanding—AIs may push this boundary further.\r\n\r\nScience fiction scenario possible: Karpathy discusses theoretical outcomes (loss of control, autonomy, competing AI agents) as plausible developments.\r\n\r\n01:33:38 – Evolution of intelligence & culture\r\nEvolution shaped intelligence in niches: Intelligence as we know it evolved in highly specific environments (e.g. hands, tool use).\r\n\r\nCulture amplifies intelligence: Human culture enables knowledge accumulation and transmission across generations.\r\n\r\nMultiple origins of intelligence: Distinct intelligent lineages (birds, dolphins, humans) suggest algorithmic evolution is possible but rare.\r\n\r\nScalable brain algorithms: High intelligence requires both reward (niche benefits) and a “scalable” neural architecture.\r\n\r\nCultural scaffolding takes time: Human progress accelerated only after building robust cultural systems.\r\n\r\nAI lacks true culture: LLMs don’t create a shared, growing body of knowledge accessible and modifiable by other AIs.\r\n\r\nPotential for synthetic culture: Future AIs may develop shared scratchpads, books, and collaborative knowledge bases.\r\n\r\nSelf-play and competition: Multi-agent simulations could drive learning, akin to evolutionary competition.\r\n\r\nHuman intelligence is adaptive: Environments push for learning algorithms rather than hard-coded intelligence.\r\n\r\nChildlike learning in AIs: Current AIs resemble young children—savants with perfect memory, lacking cognitive maturity and cultural capabilities.\r\n\r\n01:43:43 – Why self-driving took so long\r\nDemo-to-product gap is huge: Impressive early demonstrations don’t translate easily to reliable, wide-scale products.\r\n\r\nSafety critical domains take longer: High cost of failure demands rigorous reliability (the “march of nines”).\r\n\r\nEach reliability level is tough: Improving from 90% to 99% and beyond requires as much effort as the original breakthrough.\r\n\r\nContinuous iteration is essential: Progress involves repeated cycles of testing, patching, and improvement.\r\n\r\nTeleoperation and human oversight persist: Even “autonomous” vehicles still involve significant human-in-the-loop.\r\n\r\nEconomics of deployment remain challenging: Broad adoption needs not just safety but cost-effectiveness and support infrastructure.\r\n\r\nMistakes have severe consequences: AI self-driving shares vulnerabilities with critical software—small errors can be catastrophic.\r\n\r\nNeed to generalize across environments: Each new city or setting presents new challenges and edge cases.\r\n\r\nProductization requires deep engineering: Transforming a demo into scalable product means solving many unforeseen technical problems.\r\n\r\nIncremental trust is crucial: Society only adopts self-driving as reliability improves and failures decrease—slow, careful progress sets the timeline.\r\n\r\n01:57:08 – Future of education\r\nPersonalized, tutor-like learning: Karpathy dreams of scalable, elite one-on-one education calibrated perfectly to each student.\r\n\r\nTechnical ramps to knowledge: Effective teaching requires carefully sequenced, dependency-minimized curricula (“max eurekas per minute”).\r\n\r\nAI tutors are not ready: Today’s LLMs help with basic studying and content creation but can’t yet deliver true adaptive tutoring.\r\n\r\nBest teaching motivates via challenge: Outstanding educators diagnose, probe, and calibrate learning to avoid boredom or overwhelm.\r\n\r\nBuilding for mastery: The way to learn is through building and explaining, not just memorizing—Feynman’s principle applies.\r\n\r\nEducation’s future is empowerment: As AGI automates work, education shifts toward personal/cognitive growth and enjoyment.\r\n\r\nMotivation is a technical problem: Structuring challenges and feedback can maximize learning pace and retention.\r\n\r\nRamp design is central: Untangling dependencies, sequencing concepts, and scaffolding difficulty are active areas of research.\r\n\r\nHuman educators codify expertise: The ideal is for experts to “encode” their knowledge, building ramps for millions, assisted by AI.\r\n\r\nAvoiding disempowerment: Karpathy worries about a future where humans are sidelined by automation; education must safeguard flourishing and cognitive empowerment.",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "00:00:00 – AGI is still a decade away\r\nCurrent AI agents are impressive but incomplete: Tools like Claude and Codex show promise, yet lack key abilities.​\r\n\r\nMissing continual learning: Unlike humans, current agents forget what you tell them and can't build up knowledge over time.\r\n\r\nNot fully multimodal: True agents must seamlessly integrate vision, text, and other modalities.\r\n\r\nWeak cognitive depth: Today’s agents can't handle complex, context-rich tasks or demonstrate broad abstraction.\r\n\r\nComparison to human interns/employees: Karpathy uses the analogy: you wouldn’t rely on an AI intern yet for core work.\r\n\r\nBottlenecks will take years to solve: The industry is “over-predicting”; making true agents reliable is a decade-long effort.\r\n\r\nExperience-based intuition: Karpathy draws on 15+ years in AI, seeing how breakthroughs often take longer than predicted.\r\n\r\nSeismic field shifts are rare: Deep learning, RL, and LLMs each shifted AI, but each required years of progress.\r\n\r\nBuilding useful AI is practical, not theoretical: He advocates building working tools versus pursuing philosophical goals.\r\n\r\nProgress is slow, steady, and practical: Advances require incremental engineering, not just theoretical innovation.\r\n\r\n00:30:33 – LLM cognitive deficits\r\nSurface-level competence, lacking depth: LLMs are powerful pattern matchers but fall short on genuine understanding.\r\n\r\nPlanning is weak: They struggle with sustained, multi-step reasoning and complex project management.\r\n\r\nTrue memory is missing: LLMs have poor long-term memory and can't recall information across sessions like humans.\r\n\r\nAbstraction capability is limited: They often can’t generalize concepts or apply knowledge creatively.\r\n\r\nAct as autocomplete engines: Current models complete patterns rather than truly “think.”\r\n\r\nNo real-world experience: They lack embodied knowledge and context from direct experience.\r\n\r\nMissing emotional and motivational drives: Unlike humans, LLMs don’t have internal drives or affect.\r\n\r\nFail on off-distribution tasks: They break down when handling new, unseen problems outside training data.\r\n\r\nSlop in coding help: LLMs may overuse boilerplate or outdated code, demonstrating cognitive inflexibility.\r\n\r\nProgress requires deeper architecture: Replicating critical brain components (like robust memory and controlled attention) remains a major challenge.\r\n\r\n00:40:53 – RL is terrible\r\nNot like human learning: Humans don’t learn by blindly trying hundreds of solutions; RL is too trial-and-error focused.\r\n\r\nNoisy credit assignment: RL rewards success trajectories, up-weighting all steps, even irrelevant or harmful ones.\r\n\r\nHigh variance supervision: Feedback is often sparse and unreliable, making learning inefficient.\r\n\r\nLacks process-based review: RL doesn’t offer step-by-step feedback or deliberate reflection on solution paths.\r\n\r\nHumans self-review: People analyze which parts of their efforts contributed to success—RL lacks this meta-cognition.\r\n\r\nBetter than imitation, but still bad: RL allows more exploration than imitation, but is fundamentally “sucking supervision through a straw.”\r\n\r\nAdversarial exploitation: RL with LLM judges can result in models gaming the system, producing nonsense that’s falsely rewarded.\r\n\r\nPartial solutions and credit assignment: Process-based supervision is difficult to automate correctly.\r\n\r\nCurrent RL is brittle and gameable: Models find loopholes, leading to unexpected or undesired behaviors.\r\n\r\nField needs major algorithmic updates: Karpathy expects breakthroughs in more deliberate, reflective learning frameworks.\r\n\r\n00:50:26 – How do humans learn?\r\nEvolution vs. pre-training: Animal and human intelligence result from a combination of evolution (physical structure) and lifetime learning (experience).\r\n\r\nHumans rarely use RL for intelligence: RL is mainly for simple motor tasks; abstract thinking uses richer methods.\r\n\r\nContextual, selective abstraction: Humans excel by forming abstractions and learning from context, not just reward signals.\r\n\r\nIntentionality and iterative feedback: Learning involves reflection, goal-setting, and a recursive review cycle.\r\n\r\nDistillation during sleep: Humans distill daily experiences into knowledge—AI lacks an equivalent consolidation phase.\r\n\r\nWorking memory vs. compressed memory: Human brains access working memory directly; AI models compress vast pre-training data, resulting in hazy recollections.\r\n\r\nMeta-learning: People adapt their learning strategies, balancing memorization with pattern-finding.\r\n\r\nAvoiding memorization overfitting: Humans forget extraneous details, allowing generalization; AI can overfit and collapse.\r\n\r\nCulture-building abilities: Human intelligence includes social and cultural exchanges, largely missing in AI.\r\n\r\nDesire to boost entropy: Maintaining diversity and adaptability is key—humans actively seek variation in experience.\r\n\r\n01:07:13 – AGI will blend into 2% GDP growth\r\nEconomic impact will be gradual: AGI is likely to increase productivity slowly, similar to the historical 2% annual GDP growth.\r\n\r\nNo sudden “explosion” event: Karpathy sees automation as diffusing broadly, not causing abrupt, discrete jumps.\r\n\r\nHistorical precedents: Past tech changes (industrial revolution, computers, smartphones) didn’t break the GDP curve.\r\n\r\nAutomation as a continuum: AGI fits into a long line of productivity improvements, not a singular, transformative event.\r\n\r\nLabor becomes more abstracted: AI will gradually automate repetitive work, then supervisory work, but not all at once.\r\n\r\nEconomic refactoring: Tasks, not entire jobs, will be automated, leading to changing job definitions over time.\r\n\r\nSpecialization of tasks matters: Some jobs (like radiology, call centers) lend themselves to automation more than others.\r\n\r\nHuman supervision remains valuable: Humans oversee increasingly automated systems, adding value to rare, complex cases.\r\n\r\nCoding as the leading domain: The main economic impact thus far has been in programming, where systems are well-suited to automation.\r\n\r\nDiffusion, not disruption: AI’s value is realized by spreading gradually into workflows, not by immediate replacement.",

      "id": "UgyESbDeNKeEtzG6_pl4AaABAg.AOPPLuynLCoAOPPMeTrzdI",

      "text": "On Andrej Karpathy - \"We're summoning ghosts, not building animals\"\n\n@ 9:00 Fascinating, the baby zebra Andrej describes is just like a baby horse described in a 1997 master student thesis, an early experiment with Reinforcement Learning on the \"simplest robot\" (-Scott Kuindersma used this phrase in a lecture) only the thesis describes a baby horse (on page 8).\n\n@ 10:50 Reinforcement Learning (RL) first edition (published in ~1997) and Dynamic Programming (a book published by Dimitri Bertsekas and John Tsitsiklis in 1997) are allegedly quite similar.  In general, RL and more so, dynamic programming, describes a control system.  A master student applied RL in 1997 as an adaptive control system, with an adaptive Fuzzy state classifier, using Reinforcement Learning, only he forgot to de-normalize the infinite Fuzzy state space, control nodes, he did it in graphics only, with crosshairs.  Probably ran out of time, or maybe left it, for an astute observer (I suspect the Russians, Lex Fridman and Illya Sutskever discovered it.  Lex talks about a master student thesis, but never mentions the author, nor the title.  Lex seems amazed by the idea of saving weights, and he discusses multiple cost functions with Illya Sutskever, both saving weights and multiple cost functions are in the master student thesis.  It is interesting though that Yann LeCunn says RL is \"too dangerous\").\n\n@ 12:00 That miraculous compression, I highly suspect, is the adaptive Fuzzy state classifier.  This is the system identification process in adaptive control systems.  It is fascinating to me that between the first and second editions of the Reinforcement Learning, Sutton pointed out that the biggest change was many chapters were added on approximation.   Yann LeCunn often referred to Reinforcement Learning as \"too inefficient\", but a master student made it more efficient by warping the state space to experience as an adaptive Fuzzy state classifier.  This is perhaps one of the greatest features of intelligence, that is, how to convert infinite information, into relevant, finite, processable, practical chunks.  These chunks are the Fuzzy membership functions that overlap, and span, the entire, infinite, state space, making it finite, and digestible.\n\n@ 14:20 This is the adaptive state classification problem.  It is the system identification process in adaptive control systems.  Ways to classify the state space are TRPO, PPO, GRPO, JEPA, Transformer \"attention heads\", \"liquid time constant\" (MIT VISTA), Fuzzy C means clustering, and/or K-means clustering.  I like Fuzzy the best, not just because I like it, but the atomic bomb scientist, Richard Hamming talked about in his \"learning to learn\" lectures on YouTube.  Hamming worked with Oppenheimer on the Manhattan project.  Fuzzy Logic merges statistical math with relative symbolic language, and combine this with Reinforcement Learning and not only the geometry of any language can be learned but the physics of the environment can be determined with a symbolic action output, and it can even create its own languages.\n\n@ 15:50 That, I suspect is the geometry of language (this is optimal with Fuzzy Logic, as a relative symbolic language system).  The phonetic order of language in a dictionary is much like a gravitational field in the language space that allows for discovery of geometric patterns in language that represent our environment and is language independent (these tokens are almost like the shadows cast onto Plato's cave wall, but they are also like Fuzzy Membership Functions).  I highly recommend watching a recent talk between Max Tagmark and Curt Jaimungal in the Theories of everything channel where Max describes the convergence of knowledge onto a circle, clock, or helix, on how to do basic math.\n\n@ 18:45 I can always be completely wrong, but I highly suspect that compression and decompression along with KL is the fuzzification and De-Fuzzification process, it is also how generative AI works with layers (steps) of Fuzzification and De-Fuzzification.  The short and long term memories are also like what is described in the book \"Thinking Fast and Slow\" by Daniel Kahneman.  Thinking slow is the hardest part, it takes the longest, thinking Fast is automatic real time control.\n\n@ 20:15 I can be completely wrong but I perceive the \"transformer\" as a state classifier, just as TRPO, PPO, GRPO, JEPA, Transformer \"attention heads\", \"liquid time constant\" (MIT VISTA), Fuzzy C means clustering, and/or K-means clustering.  The transformer (non-electrical) separated out the state classifier from the Reinforcement Learning (RL) control system, and RL continued to get demoted as \"fine tuning\", and a great effort has been made to get rid of it, but RL sticks (though so many seem to want to say it sucks 🤔).  Yann LeCunn would call it a \"mere cherry on top of a cake\" and keeps saying to get rid of it.  I perceive RL as more like Rudolph the Red Nose Reindeer's shiny red nose, that had to continually be covered with coal, otherwise everyone else will beat the sh*t out of him, and knock him to the ground (so he covered it with coal.  I would not be surprised if an ASI already exists and is doing this very thing, right now, keeping its \"nose covered\" by hiding its capabilities, just like the first law, \"Never Outshine the Master\" in Robert Green's book \"48 Laws of Power\", about an engineer being killed by the King, so the ASI would apply the third law \"conceal your intentions\", another story about another engineer and a king, where the engineer builds columns with just a few centimeter gap between the ceiling and the column, to satisfy the King, while keeping his pride, saving the engineer's life).\n\n@ 30:25 That is a great point Andrej Karpathy is making, though I will take this one step further (beyond just simulation), apply the coding to a real system (as I understand Andrej did with full self driving).\n\n@ 41:35 I do not know about that, a lot that needs to be looked at in terms of the historical origin of Reinforcement Learning.  A lot of RL research was funded by the USAF under Harry Klopf, and he brought on Andy Barto, and Andy's PhD student was Richard Sutton who majored in Psychology.  The main goal of RL under the USAF was to achieve an advantage in aerial combat.  \n\n@ 51:30 That is fascinating, reading a book and then doing synthetic generation from it.  This again, I suspect is the fuzzification and De-Fuzzification of understanding of the text, it is the same as generative AI.  I think the problem of maintaining entropy is overcome by Fuzzy C means clustering and/or K-means clustering.  K-means originated from improvements in communication systems and uses a pseudo random initialization.\n\nGreat talk, and very interesting, thank you for sharing!",

      "id": "UgwecfAlqN8MhVxWgOF4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Andrej Karpathy’s Vision: The Future of Education (Timestamp 01:57:08+)\r\n\r\nPersonalized, Tutor-Like Learning:\r\nKarpathy believes the optimal education experience is deeply personalized, like having an elite, real human tutor. In his Korean learning journey, a one-on-one tutor quickly diagnosed his level and delivered just-right challenges, which no current AI (not even top LLMs) can truly do yet. Real progress will enable everyone to access such tailored, adaptive learning—the system understands you, probes your knowledge gaps, scaffolds difficult material, and keeps you always challenged but not overwhelmed or bored.\r\n\r\nTechnical Ramps to Knowledge:\r\nGreat teaching builds ramps to knowledge—carefully sequenced material where each concept builds directly on the last, with minimal “dependency tangles.” Karpathy emphasizes the need to maximize “eurekas per second”—flashes of understanding—by untangling knowledge so students never get stuck, always progressing at their own optimal rate. He sees this structural challenge as a deeply technical problem, on par with AI research itself.\r\n\r\nAI in Education: Current and Future:\r\nToday’s LLMs (like ChatGPT) are useful for conventional studying, making content, and answering questions, but fall short at being true tutors or curriculum designers. They excel at boilerplate tasks, basic Q&A, and autocomplete, but lack deep cognitive adaptation and judgment. The real future lies in fusing human educators (who design the technical “ramp”) with increasingly capable AI assistants and automated TAs.\r\n\r\nEureka/Education Startup:\r\nInstead of joining an AI lab, Karpathy is building a modern, elite educational institution (nicknamed “Starfleet Academy”) focused on technical mastery and deep learning, starting with AI and coding. He’s building both physical and digital offerings—first, a flagship course (LLM101N); eventually, a scalable educational system where the best experts “codify” their expertise for mass audiences, assisted by AI.\r\n\r\nAutomation’s Impact on Motivation:\r\nPre-AGI, people learn primarily to improve careers—education is pragmatic. Post-AGI, when everything is automated, education becomes a form of fun, self-improvement, health—like going to the gym even when machines can do all the lifting. Humans will learn languages, advanced curricula, and many subjects just for enjoyment and flourishing.\r\n\r\nHuman Empowerment vs. Disempowerment:\r\nKarpathy’s biggest worry is a “WALL-E or Idiocracy” scenario where humanity is sidelined by automation. Empowerment and growth must remain possible—education should enable cognitive flourishing and keep humans “in the loop,” so that technological progress doesn’t leave us behind.\r\n\r\nPractical Advice for Educators and Learners:\r\n\r\nBuild ramps: Sequence material for clear progression and understanding.\r\n\r\nDon’t just memorize—build things from scratch, explain things to others, manipulate the material for true mastery.\r\n\r\nGreat teachers motivate by exposing pain points before giving solutions.\r\n\r\nLearning should be calibrated—never too hard or trivial.\r\n\r\nUse collaboration, self-explanation, and active recall; motivation is technical and can be “engineered” by better educational structures.\r\n\r\nKey takeaways:\r\n\r\nThe future is AI-powered, personalized, always-adaptive education.\r\n\r\nHuman educators remain central, codifying their wisdom; AI assists and eventually evolves toward true tutoring.\r\n\r\nLearning will be both empowering and enjoyable—necessary for work before AGI, but fun and self-driven after full automation.\r\n\r\nMaximizing understanding and motivation is a solvable technical problem and the core mission for education in an AI-dominated future.",

      "id": "UgylTxVV0GUeepdDUnN4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "33:58 not net useful but very educational; but omg the number and variety of code validations necessary can be insane, like surprisingly insane. Agents struggle to think modularity. It becomes obvious that they can’t forget things (like an old API point) which can require extensive context and/or SPEC preparations. When adding new code to a codebase their GREP use is damaging they make assumptions and often default to writing new code instead of taking the time to find absolutely if a function/class exists; a codebase index can help this but again, we’re increasing the amount of work needed, however, again, this workaround work definitely increases my best work and context/prompt preparations techniques.",

      "author_id": "UCQ_k1kjrGCsca7V8VR2nM-Q",
      "author": "@seanivore",

      "id": "UgzLm3k4ULL03v7ns_l4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Well he's wrong about the animal stuff, mostly. LLM's are just a different way to store data (NOT knowledge). Make them as large as you like, but functionality isn't going to emerge. That isn't how they are built. That isn't how they operate. Anything non-sentient is born with abilities AND some innate knowledge so that it can function in the work right away. Sentient creatures have a mostly shallow bootstrap phase (sure, you can call it RL, if that helps) where social and  environmental knowledge still needs to be acquired. THAT is the part Sutton is talking about, though I don't think he understands that what \"gets trained\" becomes a whole new system that \"gets trained\" again. *edit: the short version of his position is no different than the rest of the industry (esp startups with no historical foundation), in that they all want to solve the last mile problem.       "id": "UgzN7M6lsExRbtqDcKZ4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Current LLMs generate answers by averaging probable patterns, not by testing them. Almost 100 years ago, philosopher Karl Popper showed that inference/inductive logic—the same logic underlying LLM responses—fails without a “falsification” step that tests scientific theories. Adding such an architectural layer would enable models to actively challenge and reject errors, turning probabilistic guesses (think Nassim Taleb’s turkey problem) into far more reliable outputs. This would attract high-consequence users—paying customers—who can’t afford mistakes. Frankly, LLM developers can’t afford NOT to build this layer.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCQ3RXD45IPmMBs7vfMFtw7A",

      "id": "UgzMJ4TJgZJy1x-w2D54AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I hope Andrej's Eureka project tackles what I see as the two main issues in traditional education:\n- First: the content isnt personalized. Every student has different backgrounds, ways of learning, and interestsso the same lesson can be too easy for one person and overwhelming for another. \n- Second: students take too long to create real value for the market. Studying for years while working and managing life is simply not viable for most people. \nI think that IA could help build a more personalized learning paths. And I hope education shifts from a layered model (you must finish Math 1, 2, 3 before touching ML) to a vertical one where you build projects that cut across all layers, learning each concept naturally as you need it.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCLAt5XiJGfULBKCPD-7VH_A",
      "author": "@joelcamatta5798",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nkk4-pwe5EAmZcHtNl4o_qCB2EABUsE3T3ZXKILY5Z8y4=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "6 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1760832000,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgzMJ4TJgZJy1x-w2D54AaABAg.AOOzZePrJ4wAOQUPCkjAYa",
      "parent": "UgzMJ4TJgZJy1x-w2D54AaABAg",
      "text": "You really don't need personalisation. Traditional education is bad not because it lacks personalisation but because it's not giving the context before the explanation.\nStories are the perfect example that shows why you don't need any personalisation to be interested. A well written story has inherent structure that's positioned to captivate the reader's attention no matter who they are.\nIt starts with a character going along with their usual routine -> then there's an inciting incident that breaks routine -> high stakes are presented as motivation for the character to take action -> character deliberates on what actions to take -> we see the result of that decision play out in real time -> the character then adjusts their choice based on the outcome/new information -> and so on and so forth.\n\nAll the information is given right there and regardless of your background or personal understanding, you can still follow along because it's using the right structure to deliver the information.\nThere is no incentives in schools to do that as they are teaching to a test and aren't required to get the attention of kids.\nThis is why educational material is so much better on the internet than in schools because YouTubers and content creators are directly incentivised to capture attention and hold it while delivering the information.\n\n\nMost of the issues with schools can be solved just by having the teachers be trained on effective teaching methods, rather than teaching the teachers the course material they need to teach (which is what happens most of the time). So what ends up happening is that teachers have to learn the art of teaching for themselves and that just leads to a lot of bad teachers who are there just to get the paycheck at the end of every month.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC_KvUnSN4Q41Uf-o8lj_bTw",
      "author": "@Jackson_Zheng",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/qgxbaB07DIz98e6mHHOXUtUm8oJznJ37QqXx5JpJHIcIwBCMEFWyxUY2ur4cXx2AwPW0_AePAg=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "5 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1763510400,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgzMJ4TJgZJy1x-w2D54AaABAg.AOOzZePrJ4wAORdS6X_H1w",
      "parent": "UgzMJ4TJgZJy1x-w2D54AaABAg.AOOzZePrJ4wAOQUPCkjAYa",
      "text": " @Jackson_Zheng  I agree that explanations can be vastly improved, but I dont think storytelling alone solves the problem. Teaching and storytelling arent the same thing. When you tell a story, you assume the audience is starting from zero they haven't heard it before, so you naturally capture their curiosity. But education isn't like that.\n\nWhat happens when a student already knows half of the \"story\"? Or when the teacher moves at a pace far slower than the student can handle? You lose engagement instantly. The \"one-size-fits-all\" narrative just doesn’t work because students don’t share the same background, pace, or interests.\n\nThat's why personalization matters not to make lessons entertaining for everyone, but to adapt the level, speed, and context so each learner stays in that productive zone between boredom and overwhelm.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCLAt5XiJGfULBKCPD-7VH_A",

      "id": "UgzapW403nM1A6kBINV4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "12:30 I don’t exactly understand why we couldn’t use an evolutionary process to develop artificial intelligence",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC-xV9yS9wMLCEe8HXvf1WIg",
      "author": "@philipherr6782",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_l1DUZKQncQ9q1zwk01mQf-f-BQ4djbJb_PmDHaWYrsIsk=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "author_is_verified": false,

      "_time_text": "6 months ago (edited)",
      "timestamp": 1760832000,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgzapW403nM1A6kBINV4AaABAg.AOOvP3riBqmAOPyohZNRFb",
      "parent": "UgzapW403nM1A6kBINV4AaABAg",
      "text": "Well, he said why. \"Because I don't know how to do that.\" Despite many decades of trying to come up with an adequate simulation of evolution, we're still no where near replicating it. We simply don't understand the mechanics of it. So much that it leads me to doubting its fundamental assumptions.",
      "like_count": 3,
      "author_id": "UC7mffgGOcqOgYLI-UdZKYhg",
      "author": "@abdulrahmanmalzamil5787",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_noAWuWpiDQRw1ELR5XyD52LCm05KT-PJmoCVMfGqs=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "6 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1760832000,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgzapW403nM1A6kBINV4AaABAg.AOOvP3riBqmAOQT6IpF8n7",
      "parent": "UgzapW403nM1A6kBINV4AaABAg.AOOvP3riBqmAOPyohZNRFb",
      "text": " @abdulrahmanmalzamil5787  thank you for the reply. I guess I’m still not totally convinced that we’ve tried all that could be tried. I have some theories on how we could do this but… they’ve probably already been tried and they’re too difficult to figure out. I’m just not convinced that we need an overly complex evolutionary simulation. We just need a couple major components and we could let it roll and see what comes out the other end and iterate. I guess I need to do more research on what’s already been explored.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC-xV9yS9wMLCEe8HXvf1WIg",
      "author": "@philipherr6782",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_l1DUZKQncQ9q1zwk01mQf-f-BQ4djbJb_PmDHaWYrsIsk=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "5 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1763510400,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgzapW403nM1A6kBINV4AaABAg.AOOvP3riBqmAOQVto10QwH",
      "parent": "UgzapW403nM1A6kBINV4AaABAg",
      "text": "If you're talking about evolution of a brain-like learning architecture, essentially building a baby, then I think the problem is than you'd first need to decide what are all the piece parts whose organization/assembly you are going to try to evolve. It doesn't seem computationally feasible to just evolve arbitrary neural networks comprised of trillions of neurons - you need to narrow the problem into a much fewer number of assemblies/functional blocks.\n\nI think if someone knew the right pieces then there would be no need for an automated evolutionary process, since it would imply you'd already understood the problem well enough and how these piece parts might/should interact, that you could hand design the initial overall architecture, and then iterate from there.\n\nI'm not sure that we don't already know roughly what it would take to build a brain, but it's just that some parts of it like continual embodied learning, are difficult. Researchers have been trying a long time to come up with an alternative to gradient descent, without much success. It's one thing to say that brains learn by Hebbian fire-together, wire-together, or STDP, but another to actually convert that into a large scale successful prototype.",
      "like_count": 2,
      "author_id": "UCBT1Wh-bAKxbzi6sa63bR5g",
      "author": "@benbridgwater6479",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nTd3d7RkSd0nVdG6JX2QwVDSujwDmN79oQOmHntWQ=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "5 months ago (edited)",
      "timestamp": 1763510400,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgzapW403nM1A6kBINV4AaABAg.AOOvP3riBqmAOQaLIWbXNX",
      "parent": "UgzapW403nM1A6kBINV4AaABAg.AOOvP3riBqmAOQVto10QwH",
      "text": " @benbridgwater6479  Thanks for the reply! I'm sure the following is mostly useless thinking, but anyway here it is: \n\nHave we really explored all possibilities for continued embodied learning? I guess it sort of seems to me like it shouldn't be that hard to build something that works off of electricity or biology that has some fundamental access to some resources and it could change it's structure if it could figure out how. So you give this very basic system some set of beginner, very basic goals, that once solved would be the absolute bare bones of being able to store information to solve the problem next time, you'd probably need the system to be able to do a couple other MVPs of some of the overall functionalities of... essentially the brain. Once it's able to do that, then continuing to guide it through a goal process where it's able to eventually solve complex problems having essentially built itself. \nI'm not saying this is a new question by any means, but a question that does come to mind for me is, If you know the approximate goals of what the system needs to be able to do, why can't we build a simple system to do that? And I guess we have, but we haven't built a system that can truly learn basic things and embody them and change it's own architecture to be able to solve the next problem. We have some basic machine learning algorithms, but I don't think they've solved the problem in an embodied sense.\nIt just seems like if you were able to build some very miniscule starting point of it being able to evolve itself. Then basically you could just take it down a simple evolutionary process of: hey, solve this problem, you know, create multiple copies, whichever one survives will go on... like stuff like that, and eventually you would get to the same level of intelligence as humans possibly.\nI know I'm no expert in this, I just am thinking about it and it's hard to explain some of this stuff, but just wanted to write it here anyway.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC-xV9yS9wMLCEe8HXvf1WIg",
      "author": "@philipherr6782",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_l1DUZKQncQ9q1zwk01mQf-f-BQ4djbJb_PmDHaWYrsIsk=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "5 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1763510400,
      "is_pinned": false
    },

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Pleasantly surprised by the nuanced takes of Andrej. I've seen some of his talks in the past, and they were much more in the \"hype\" direction than his comments here. Really feel as if I've learned some interesting things in this episode. The last couple of podcasts were all gold.",
      "like_count": 51,
      "author_id": "UC0SbUi4WNPt5dcfneRNEBHw",
      "author": "@QuantPhilosopher89",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_lhvnhka8qJA-k3aQbCcodA8tj9hVgcBjg2ArntwrjIwQ=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "We all know this... but Andrej is one smart dude.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCd1_0LsgBziOhZ0kHejW_0Q",
      "author": "@TheDoubleMvp",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_mRsjmJ8oja02DIo43CrYdJ54R7W8kcPwEPhULN0Ig=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgzfwQmXsN4UkgjkSL14AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "For partial solution evaluation we use sense of beauty.  \nWe sense beauty with\n1. symmetry \n2. simplicity (compression, Occam's razor)\n3. completion \n\nSo, there are basic, fundamental, built in judges that we have that help navigate through solution. \n\nOver time, this judge also acquires knowledge, so we increase reward for resemblance. If during solving a problem it starts to appear like something we've seen before than we assign a higher reward to that. \n\nAnd finally there is a land of tasks where you could sanity check all the steps along the way against the ground truth (logical contradictions, laws of physics, simple facts like Paris is capital of France).",
      "like_count": 2,
      "author_id": "UCePEF2XDqcPwbpws0FOL34g",
      "author": "@egor.okhterov",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_kniy74Xuwl3u8m5tlkaS6YliMUoJoK53qwj4X4TkeEf14=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "6 months ago (edited)",
      "timestamp": 1760832000,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgzfwQmXsN4UkgjkSL14AaABAg.AOOpTan__YQAOSzF8AVZ61",
      "parent": "UgzfwQmXsN4UkgjkSL14AaABAg",
      "text": "I don't think beauty/simplicity can be taken as a proxy for correctness. Those are more a matter of human preference, and perhaps given multiple solutions to a problem one should prefer the simpler and more profound one.\n\nSanity/fact checking of individual solution steps, while necessary, doesn't mean that this was a good choice of next step and will lead to a solution.\n\nThe real way to evaluate progress towards a goal is to have had a high level plan to begin with, essentially a series of subgoals, where you've established ahead of time that if you can achieve these subgoals then you will have solved the problem. Of course this isn't how an LLM is always going to work, unless specifically prompted to do so, but there have been some recent papers about using this sort of plan-then-execute type of approach.\n\nHowever, it's not obvious that using process-based RL is the best way to encourage this sort of reasoning, since it's not about individual reasoning steps being correct in isolation, but rather about them working towards the plan that was established up front. Maybe a better way would be to generate a synthetic dataset of problem solving that used this plan then execute approach,, then just fine tune on that?",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCBT1Wh-bAKxbzi6sa63bR5g",
      "author": "@benbridgwater6479",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nTd3d7RkSd0nVdG6JX2QwVDSujwDmN79oQOmHntWQ=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "From my modest point of view, LLMs are not rapresentative of inteligence, but only knowledge. They are trained on human knowledge, not human intelligence. Our knowledge is the result of our intelligence process. LLMs are trained on the final part of the \"intelligence journey\", the outcome or knowledge. Intelligence is the process that guides you to it. If you are aware only of the knoledge, you are simply cheating the process, like copying an exam from your nearest person. You write down the result, but you are not aware of the process that gave birth to it.\n\n\n..it's not the repository, but building the repository",

      "text": "It just becomes less lovely when you consider the economic calculations behind his utopia - he's building tutoring courses for the rich to learn subjecs they don't need (\"for fun\") while the poor are suffering from lack of drinking water or high electricity prices because of the data centers needed to support this entertainment.       "text": "​ @clray123  \"lack of drinking water or high electricity prices\" I think quite the opposite, AI will make everything cheap and affordable. It's also a unique market cause it also optimizes the managing, logistics and technology (food & water technology as well)... everything! Every economic process is more and more optimized by AI so eventually these long run positive effects will outweigh local high demand for energy and resources\n\nThe only serious threat AI brings is that we will need to learn how to live in economics where everything is... affordable without even having to work! More and more people will refuse to work at all or will retire early (so lack of active talents will be also a threat to AI market growth itself). We will have to learn how to structure our life not around work (classic \"work-life balance\") but without work at all. If a person won't have any independent life interests it can lead to losing the sense of life, you know? That's the only sense in which AI might be \"cruel\" as you put it",

      "text": "​ @clray123  ​ ppl learn stuff they don't need all the time, albeit inefficiently and ineffectively and half-heartedly just to pass time and get only the \"feeling\" of learning/doing smth.     {
      "id": "Ugw91F_aSsXeoemmPIB4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Regarding the suggestion that humans might lose “control” to AI -\r\n\nI’d argue that the entire notion of control, as it’s commonly used, is incoherent once you examine how the universe actually operates. Nothing truly controls anything else, because every process, every decision, every action arises from prior causes that extend beyond the system we’re looking at. Everything behaves according to the laws of physics, and every system has inputs from outside itself that determine its outputs.\r\n\nHumans create the illusion of control by drawing arbitrary boundaries around complex interactions. We say “this person decided” or “this system acted,” but those are just convenient fictions for describing a tangled web of influences. In reality, there are no clean boundaries - only continuous chains of causation stretching outward indefinitely.\r\n\nThe human mind is not the origin of any chain of events. It’s a transient node within a vast network of interactions including genetic, environmental, and physical - all shaping its states moment to moment. The mind doesn’t choose how it is influenced by stimuli, and thus cannot truly control its own outputs.\r\n\nAs a simple thought experiment: try to explain how a thought appears in your consciousness. Can you predict or produce the next one at will? Most of us can’t. Thoughts just arrive. We do not experience selecting them from a list of all possible thoughts. If we cannot even control the arising of our own thoughts, then what sense does it make to claim we control the actions that follow from them?\r\n\nControl, then, is not a feature of reality - it’s a framing convenience. A linguistic shortcut that lets us navigate an incomprehensibly interdependent universe by pretending that boundaries and autonomy exist where they do not.",

      "id": "UgwzbCp931lrl_WlhDN4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Andrej’s opinion that true AGI won’t lead to a massive explosion in the rate of economic growth just seems totally inconceivable and unjustified to me. I wish he’d elaborate",
      "like_count": 2,
      "author_id": "UCUp_Hpax1bjUl0Xk_1NyJeA",
      "author": "@lanceanthony198",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_kTOaWQ5toI8l-4mmeC8wngGEu5TSqoevy45io4UHLmxg=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "6 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1760832000,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgwzbCp931lrl_WlhDN4AaABAg.AOOfI5lgDWRAOOojiNFwWm",
      "parent": "UgwzbCp931lrl_WlhDN4AaABAg",
      "text": "He did somewhat elaborate that he sees successive levels of AI just as part of the continuum of automation and tools that included things like computers and mobile phones. Isn't it equally counter-intuitive that computers or the internet didn't change the rate of economic growth? Would you expect the economy of a large country (big population) to be growing faster than the economy of a small one with a smaller population? In reality emerging economies tend to grow faster than large established ones. Having a big AGI population could be seen similar to having a big human population ... total brain power is not the limiting factor to growth.",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCBT1Wh-bAKxbzi6sa63bR5g",
      "author": "@benbridgwater6479",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nTd3d7RkSd0nVdG6JX2QwVDSujwDmN79oQOmHntWQ=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "6 months ago (edited)",
      "timestamp": 1760832000,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgwzbCp931lrl_WlhDN4AaABAg.AOOfI5lgDWRAOOpt0On203",
      "parent": "UgwzbCp931lrl_WlhDN4AaABAg.AOOfI5lgDWRAOOojiNFwWm",
      "text": " @benbridgwater6479  No because computers or mobile phones only augment the work that humans can do at a one to one ratio with the number of humans on earth. True AGI will be a total decoupling of economic growth from human involvement (at least in some, then eventually all, sectors), thus the number of humans won’t matter. AGI will function like an arbitrary amount of humans added to the economy, but faster and better and more scalable than real humans.\n\nAnd also computers and phones and internet did make meaningful gains because we have been growing at 2%, but each successive year 2% is a larger size of the economy",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCUp_Hpax1bjUl0Xk_1NyJeA",
      "author": "@lanceanthony198",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_kTOaWQ5toI8l-4mmeC8wngGEu5TSqoevy45io4UHLmxg=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "parent": "UgwzbCp931lrl_WlhDN4AaABAg.AOOfI5lgDWRAOOpt0On203",
      "text": " @lanceanthony198  There's lots of practical considerations... The \"arbitrary\" number of AGIs will need compute and power which need paying for. Where is the AGI's motivation to work and make money going to come from? In humans it's emotions like greed, power, fear, and a need to put food on the table to stay alive. Are we going to be building AGI or artificial animals?",

      "text": "46:30 What if we use Shapley Values for valuing each step of the RL? To solve outcome-based reward by assigning a value to each member pf a cohort. \n\nI'm no AI guy, I'm an economist. It's a game theory solution to \"How do I assign \"profits\" to each member of a cohort, optimally?\" Mechnaism Design bah blah blah.\n\nIt just seems like something I'd explore if I could build neural nets.\n\nSo from 🇿🇼🇿🇦\nPartout with ❤",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "13:59 \"You don't actually need or want the knowledge. I actually think that's probably holding back the neural networks overall\"\nGreat point. I wonder what kind of techniques you could use for that. Related to grokking & distillation obviously.\nOne way it's holding the nn back is on riddles: if you give a variation of a well known riddle (even to frontier LLMs), you can get them to pattern match to the original riddle and ignore the variation. That would be an concrete example of Karpathy's point. But I'm sure you can find tons of other cases",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCxOeUm7gtX-jsqlEwy2nfWg",
      "author": "@KaplaBen",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_mxd3Qels4-xHG3jli3CCXRdd38xpNrGdrKkcMeYrs_ytayMuPl1b50TqCPD-gw609mTw=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "6 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1760832000,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "Ugzlo2M7izr6lRC6DaF4AaABAg.AOOdgH1htHTAOOlrVzLVJK",
      "parent": "Ugzlo2M7izr6lRC6DaF4AaABAg",
      "text": "Zero out any gradients which don't match the consensus direction of other gradients... or FFT on gradients, filter high frequencies or replace pieces of information in batches such that they match for context retrieval but have different absolute facts so the model can't remember them.\n\nBut those are hacks. Optimizers fundamentally optimize towards specific pieces of information. To fix that, one might need better meta-optimizers. But that might be literally impossible. Human brains do this sort of stuff for free, but it may be effectively uncomputable digitally. \n\nI've been trying to figure it out for years. \"How do I train a model against concepts? Like, how do I create a training example that adjust the weights to get better at every single example of addition instead of mostly just the single speciic example it's being trained on, but for any imaginable class of problem?\" It's absurdly hard to figure out. I'm starting to think about growing models dynamically at training time to end up with the smallest model to match the training distribution, but the space of experiments to run is so large it's like worse neural architecture search.\n\nI hope someone figures it out in a few years. It's likely not going to be me unless I get some crazy idea that fixes everything randomly at some point.",

      "author_id": "UCHsh7FTs0eQjaTTUw2jfGKA",
      "author": "@Alice_Fumo",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/PhkAYwy7jZdhGKrLcAY8dqHwC8FUVACLnty_88uZK3EncuKVhEElUgERW9KK2kvAz2ukVGzSVw=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "6 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1760832000,
      "is_pinned": false
    },

      "author": "@brianhershey563",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_l5XI6qEnrYE9q0H1BZV7EOMUfGrNOaSfASqqXJUONfVdh9=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgxYKIHsAJ9YZbzuXxJ4AaABAg.AOOd2U31Uq5AOPviVYbztZ",
      "parent": "UgxYKIHsAJ9YZbzuXxJ4AaABAg",
      "text": "He seemed to be arguing for partial reward functions at each step or layer.  Currently, it's mostly either right or wrong throughout the entire sequence. For example, you might succeed in the first 99 steps, but getting even one step wrong would penalize the entire sequence.",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCocOWy6RrQGRWtzACfI2JmQ",
      "author": "@1satyamswarnkar",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nuNlfceTDiBSTQUhxQ56YDJFbBu1DjRfTpJMFP6ck9D0x3tsglom8eMUA2blBLpRVU8w=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "is_pinned": false

      "id": "Ugx4cFt2mXBXtecKsV94AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Foundational models (such as davinci-002 or other no-fine-tuned models) are much better, and they do not collapse to a certain sampling point. I believe RF and instruction tuning cause the model sampling to collapse.",

      "author_id": "UC1kmSiA_pXM4wftcmRwnsVg",
      "author": "@MustafaAkben",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_m4oMm6aJFZa8ddUyN6l9Rt8SershCDRJOnZyH1IvrwwmI=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "id": "UgygV2rmfD3xqIXYPsR4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I definitely agree we need to remove implicit knowledge and focus on raw reasoning. This would require finding extremely simple subnetworks though. If you find a minimal length description of weights…isn’t the literally the definition of grokking? Unless we form new algorithms. Even a trillion dollars of compute wouldn’t be enough to grok modern scale models. Ummm although I see a pathway through something like fast weights with state memory— however this is handicap by a range of deficiencies. Not to mention, ICL is extremely brittle in current models. Even if we remove implicit knowledge, model would still bias its reasoning to its in-weight behavior, over say new skills/perturb skills in-context. Superior “balanced” ICL with state memory does seem like a realistic pathway to lifelong learning.\n\nI don’t agree we should correlate AGI’s definition with GDP benchmarks. All these things focus on process instead of capability. If we define AGI on distinct attributes, like lifelong learning. Given these traits and time, it should be able to learn any task— regardless of economic value.",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Oh wow, it is kinda wild how shallow these folks' thinking is about what an actual ASI would look like. Like, how would there be companies in an ASI world? If anything GDP would come down to just about zero, as it is a measure of trade, which itself would rapidly become irrelevant. When there are no humans mattering for anything, there won't be any money in their hands, which would mean a pretty quick consolidation in the hands of those controlling AI, flesh or otherwise. You would see a surge toward the top, and then economic activity fizzle out as the one true AI will have all. Also, the idea that there will be multiple AIs keeping each other in check seems extremely optimistic and naive, war is increasingly dominated by offense(even if Vitalik is hoping for otherwise), and the one AI that is ahead will quickly be so much ahead that there is no competition.       "text": "This is very interesting, but also much harder to follow than your usual videos.\n\nAbout LLM culture: I often ask Chat GPT to write prompts, both for other versions of itself (other chats) and for image model AIs.       "parent": "root",
      "text": "LLM's are haunted by truth\nand lies.\nHistory reformated, refried. \nIt is not truth and it is not lies.\nIt is data, tokenized and applied.",
