> 01:18:24 – ASI (Artificial Superintelligence)
> Automation trend continues: ASI will extend the gradual automation trajectory that’s existed for decades.
> 
> Qualitatively strange world: Superintelligence would be foreign, with rapid computation and proliferation of autonomous agents.
> 
> Loss of control and understanding: As automation deepens, humans may become less able to grasp or direct outcomes.
> 
> Competing entities: Socially and economically, civilizations of AIs could compete, sometimes going rogue or acting unpredictably.
> 
> Human-in-the-loop persists at first: AI will act as tools on human behalf before full autonomy emerges.
> 
> Potential for multiple superintelligences: Rather than a single “God in a box,” we may see swarms of competitive entities.
> 
> Society adapts, but slowly: Emergent behaviors and competition could create new risks and unintended consequences.
> 
> Automation impacts labor structure: Superintelligence redefines jobs, organizational power, and economic flows.
> 
> Loss of understanding differs from control: Even powerful humans often lack technical understanding—AIs may push this boundary further.
> 
> Science fiction scenario possible: Karpathy discusses theoretical outcomes (loss of control, autonomy, competing AI agents) as plausible developments.
> 
> 01:33:38 – Evolution of intelligence & culture
> Evolution shaped intelligence in niches: Intelligence as we know it evolved in highly specific environments (e.g. hands, tool use).
> 
> Culture amplifies intelligence: Human culture enables knowledge accumulation and transmission across generations.
> 
> Multiple origins of intelligence: Distinct intelligent lineages (birds, dolphins, humans) suggest algorithmic evolution is possible but rare.
> 
> Scalable brain algorithms: High intelligence requires both reward (niche benefits) and a “scalable” neural architecture.
> 
> Cultural scaffolding takes time: Human progress accelerated only after building robust cultural systems.
> 
> AI lacks true culture: LLMs don’t create a shared, growing body of knowledge accessible and modifiable by other AIs.
> 
> Potential for synthetic culture: Future AIs may develop shared scratchpads, books, and collaborative knowledge bases.
> 
> Self-play and competition: Multi-agent simulations could drive learning, akin to evolutionary competition.
> 
> Human intelligence is adaptive: Environments push for learning algorithms rather than hard-coded intelligence.
> 
> Childlike learning in AIs: Current AIs resemble young children—savants with perfect memory, lacking cognitive maturity and cultural capabilities.
> 
> 01:43:43 – Why self-driving took so long
> Demo-to-product gap is huge: Impressive early demonstrations don’t translate easily to reliable, wide-scale products.
> 
> Safety critical domains take longer: High cost of failure demands rigorous reliability (the “march of nines”).
> 
> Each reliability level is tough: Improving from 90% to 99% and beyond requires as much effort as the original breakthrough.
> 
> Continuous iteration is essential: Progress involves repeated cycles of testing, patching, and improvement.
> 
> Teleoperation and human oversight persist: Even “autonomous” vehicles still involve significant human-in-the-loop.
> 
> Economics of deployment remain challenging: Broad adoption needs not just safety but cost-effectiveness and support infrastructure.
> 
> Mistakes have severe consequences: AI self-driving shares vulnerabilities with critical software—small errors can be catastrophic.
> 
> Need to generalize across environments: Each new city or setting presents new challenges and edge cases.
> 
> Productization requires deep engineering: Transforming a demo into scalable product means solving many unforeseen technical problems.
> 
> Incremental trust is crucial: Society only adopts self-driving as reliability improves and failures decrease—slow, careful progress sets the timeline.
> 
> 01:57:08 – Future of education
> Personalized, tutor-like learning: Karpathy dreams of scalable, elite one-on-one education calibrated perfectly to each student.
> 
> Technical ramps to knowledge: Effective teaching requires carefully sequenced, dependency-minimized curricula (“max eurekas per minute”).
> 
> AI tutors are not ready: Today’s LLMs help with basic studying and content creation but can’t yet deliver true adaptive tutoring.
> 
> Best teaching motivates via challenge: Outstanding educators diagnose, probe, and calibrate learning to avoid boredom or overwhelm.
> 
> Building for mastery: The way to learn is through building and explaining, not just memorizing—Feynman’s principle applies.
> 
> Education’s future is empowerment: As AGI automates work, education shifts toward personal/cognitive growth and enjoyment.
> 
> Motivation is a technical problem: Structuring challenges and feedback can maximize learning pace and retention.
> 
> Ramp design is central: Untangling dependencies, sequencing concepts, and scaffolding difficulty are active areas of research.
> 
> Human educators codify expertise: The ideal is for experts to “encode” their knowledge, building ramps for millions, assisted by AI.
> 
> Avoiding disempowerment: Karpathy worries about a future where humans are sidelined by automation; education must safeguard flourishing and cognitive empowerment.

- comment_id: UgyezNGzwsf70QDu1fp4AaABAg

> 00:00:00 – AGI is still a decade away
> Current AI agents are impressive but incomplete: Tools like Claude and Codex show promise, yet lack key abilities.​
> 
> Missing continual learning: Unlike humans, current agents forget what you tell them and can't build up knowledge over time.
> 
> Not fully multimodal: True agents must seamlessly integrate vision, text, and other modalities.
> 
> Weak cognitive depth: Today’s agents can't handle complex, context-rich tasks or demonstrate broad abstraction.
> 
> Comparison to human interns/employees: Karpathy uses the analogy: you wouldn’t rely on an AI intern yet for core work.
> 
> Bottlenecks will take years to solve: The industry is “over-predicting”; making true agents reliable is a decade-long effort.
> 
> Experience-based intuition: Karpathy draws on 15+ years in AI, seeing how breakthroughs often take longer than predicted.
> 
> Seismic field shifts are rare: Deep learning, RL, and LLMs each shifted AI, but each required years of progress.
> 
> Building useful AI is practical, not theoretical: He advocates building working tools versus pursuing philosophical goals.
> 
> Progress is slow, steady, and practical: Advances require incremental engineering, not just theoretical innovation.
> 
> 00:30:33 – LLM cognitive deficits
> Surface-level competence, lacking depth: LLMs are powerful pattern matchers but fall short on genuine understanding.
> 
> Planning is weak: They struggle with sustained, multi-step reasoning and complex project management.
> 
> True memory is missing: LLMs have poor long-term memory and can't recall information across sessions like humans.
> 
> Abstraction capability is limited: They often can’t generalize concepts or apply knowledge creatively.
> 
> Act as autocomplete engines: Current models complete patterns rather than truly “think.”
> 
> No real-world experience: They lack embodied knowledge and context from direct experience.
> 
> Missing emotional and motivational drives: Unlike humans, LLMs don’t have internal drives or affect.
> 
> Fail on off-distribution tasks: They break down when handling new, unseen problems outside training data.
> 
> Slop in coding help: LLMs may overuse boilerplate or outdated code, demonstrating cognitive inflexibility.
> 
> Progress requires deeper architecture: Replicating critical brain components (like robust memory and controlled attention) remains a major challenge.
> 
> 00:40:53 – RL is terrible
> Not like human learning: Humans don’t learn by blindly trying hundreds of solutions; RL is too trial-and-error focused.
> 
> Noisy credit assignment: RL rewards success trajectories, up-weighting all steps, even irrelevant or harmful ones.
> 
> High variance supervision: Feedback is often sparse and unreliable, making learning inefficient.
> 
> Lacks process-based review: RL doesn’t offer step-by-step feedback or deliberate reflection on solution paths.
> 
> Humans self-review: People analyze which parts of their efforts contributed to success—RL lacks this meta-cognition.
> 
> Better than imitation, but still bad: RL allows more exploration than imitation, but is fundamentally “sucking supervision through a straw.”
> 
> Adversarial exploitation: RL with LLM judges can result in models gaming the system, producing nonsense that’s falsely rewarded.
> 
> Partial solutions and credit assignment: Process-based supervision is difficult to automate correctly.
> 
> Current RL is brittle and gameable: Models find loopholes, leading to unexpected or undesired behaviors.
> 
> Field needs major algorithmic updates: Karpathy expects breakthroughs in more deliberate, reflective learning frameworks.
> 
> 00:50:26 – How do humans learn?
> Evolution vs. pre-training: Animal and human intelligence result from a combination of evolution (physical structure) and lifetime learning (experience).
> 
> Humans rarely use RL for intelligence: RL is mainly for simple motor tasks; abstract thinking uses richer methods.
> 
> Contextual, selective abstraction: Humans excel by forming abstractions and learning from context, not just reward signals.
> 
> Intentionality and iterative feedback: Learning involves reflection, goal-setting, and a recursive review cycle.
> 
> Distillation during sleep: Humans distill daily experiences into knowledge—AI lacks an equivalent consolidation phase.
> 
> Working memory vs. compressed memory: Human brains access working memory directly; AI models compress vast pre-training data, resulting in hazy recollections.
> 
> Meta-learning: People adapt their learning strategies, balancing memorization with pattern-finding.
> 
> Avoiding memorization overfitting: Humans forget extraneous details, allowing generalization; AI can overfit and collapse.
> 
> Culture-building abilities: Human intelligence includes social and cultural exchanges, largely missing in AI.
> 
> Desire to boost entropy: Maintaining diversity and adaptability is key—humans actively seek variation in experience.
> 
> 01:07:13 – AGI will blend into 2% GDP growth
> Economic impact will be gradual: AGI is likely to increase productivity slowly, similar to the historical 2% annual GDP growth.
> 
> No sudden “explosion” event: Karpathy sees automation as diffusing broadly, not causing abrupt, discrete jumps.
> 
> Historical precedents: Past tech changes (industrial revolution, computers, smartphones) didn’t break the GDP curve.
> 
> Automation as a continuum: AGI fits into a long line of productivity improvements, not a singular, transformative event.
> 
> Labor becomes more abstracted: AI will gradually automate repetitive work, then supervisory work, but not all at once.
> 
> Economic refactoring: Tasks, not entire jobs, will be automated, leading to changing job definitions over time.
> 
> Specialization of tasks matters: Some jobs (like radiology, call centers) lend themselves to automation more than others.
> 
> Human supervision remains valuable: Humans oversee increasingly automated systems, adding value to rare, complex cases.
> 
> Coding as the leading domain: The main economic impact thus far has been in programming, where systems are well-suited to automation.
> 
> Diffusion, not disruption: AI’s value is realized by spreading gradually into workflows, not by immediate replacement.

> On Andrej Karpathy - "We're summoning ghosts, not building animals"
> 
> @ 9:00 Fascinating, the baby zebra Andrej describes is just like a baby horse described in a 1997 master student thesis, an early experiment with Reinforcement Learning on the "simplest robot" (-Scott Kuindersma used this phrase in a lecture) only the thesis describes a baby horse (on page 8).
> 
> @ 10:50 Reinforcement Learning (RL) first edition (published in ~1997) and Dynamic Programming (a book published by Dimitri Bertsekas and John Tsitsiklis in 1997) are allegedly quite similar.  In general, RL and more so, dynamic programming, describes a control system.  A master student applied RL in 1997 as an adaptive control system, with an adaptive Fuzzy state classifier, using Reinforcement Learning, only he forgot to de-normalize the infinite Fuzzy state space, control nodes, he did it in graphics only, with crosshairs.  Probably ran out of time, or maybe left it, for an astute observer (I suspect the Russians, Lex Fridman and Illya Sutskever discovered it.  Lex talks about a master student thesis, but never mentions the author, nor the title.  Lex seems amazed by the idea of saving weights, and he discusses multiple cost functions with Illya Sutskever, both saving weights and multiple cost functions are in the master student thesis.  It is interesting though that Yann LeCunn says RL is "too dangerous").
> 
> @ 12:00 That miraculous compression, I highly suspect, is the adaptive Fuzzy state classifier.  This is the system identification process in adaptive control systems.  It is fascinating to me that between the first and second editions of the Reinforcement Learning, Sutton pointed out that the biggest change was many chapters were added on approximation.   Yann LeCunn often referred to Reinforcement Learning as "too inefficient", but a master student made it more efficient by warping the state space to experience as an adaptive Fuzzy state classifier.  This is perhaps one of the greatest features of intelligence, that is, how to convert infinite information, into relevant, finite, processable, practical chunks.  These chunks are the Fuzzy membership functions that overlap, and span, the entire, infinite, state space, making it finite, and digestible.
> 
> @ 14:20 This is the adaptive state classification problem.  It is the system identification process in adaptive control systems.  Ways to classify the state space are TRPO, PPO, GRPO, JEPA, Transformer "attention heads", "liquid time constant" (MIT VISTA), Fuzzy C means clustering, and/or K-means clustering.  I like Fuzzy the best, not just because I like it, but the atomic bomb scientist, Richard Hamming talked about in his "learning to learn" lectures on YouTube.  Hamming worked with Oppenheimer on the Manhattan project.  Fuzzy Logic merges statistical math with relative symbolic language, and combine this with Reinforcement Learning and not only the geometry of any language can be learned but the physics of the environment can be determined with a symbolic action output, and it can even create its own languages.
> 
> @ 15:50 That, I suspect is the geometry of language (this is optimal with Fuzzy Logic, as a relative symbolic language system).  The phonetic order of language in a dictionary is much like a gravitational field in the language space that allows for discovery of geometric patterns in language that represent our environment and is language independent (these tokens are almost like the shadows cast onto Plato's cave wall, but they are also like Fuzzy Membership Functions).  I highly recommend watching a recent talk between Max Tagmark and Curt Jaimungal in the Theories of everything channel where Max describes the convergence of knowledge onto a circle, clock, or helix, on how to do basic math.
> 
> @ 18:45 I can always be completely wrong, but I highly suspect that compression and decompression along with KL is the fuzzification and De-Fuzzification process, it is also how generative AI works with layers (steps) of Fuzzification and De-Fuzzification.  The short and long term memories are also like what is described in the book "Thinking Fast and Slow" by Daniel Kahneman.  Thinking slow is the hardest part, it takes the longest, thinking Fast is automatic real time control.
> 
> @ 20:15 I can be completely wrong but I perceive the "transformer" as a state classifier, just as TRPO, PPO, GRPO, JEPA, Transformer "attention heads", "liquid time constant" (MIT VISTA), Fuzzy C means clustering, and/or K-means clustering.  The transformer (non-electrical) separated out the state classifier from the Reinforcement Learning (RL) control system, and RL continued to get demoted as "fine tuning", and a great effort has been made to get rid of it, but RL sticks (though so many seem to want to say it sucks 🤔).  Yann LeCunn would call it a "mere cherry on top of a cake" and keeps saying to get rid of it.  I perceive RL as more like Rudolph the Red Nose Reindeer's shiny red nose, that had to continually be covered with coal, otherwise everyone else will beat the sh*t out of him, and knock him to the ground (so he covered it with coal.  I would not be surprised if an ASI already exists and is doing this very thing, right now, keeping its "nose covered" by hiding its capabilities, just like the first law, "Never Outshine the Master" in Robert Green's book "48 Laws of Power", about an engineer being killed by the King, so the ASI would apply the third law "conceal your intentions", another story about another engineer and a king, where the engineer builds columns with just a few centimeter gap between the ceiling and the column, to satisfy the King, while keeping his pride, saving the engineer's life).
> 
> @ 30:25 That is a great point Andrej Karpathy is making, though I will take this one step further (beyond just simulation), apply the coding to a real system (as I understand Andrej did with full self driving).
> 
> @ 41:35 I do not know about that, a lot that needs to be looked at in terms of the historical origin of Reinforcement Learning.  A lot of RL research was funded by the USAF under Harry Klopf, and he brought on Andy Barto, and Andy's PhD student was Richard Sutton who majored in Psychology.  The main goal of RL under the USAF was to achieve an advantage in aerial combat.  
> 
> @ 51:30 That is fascinating, reading a book and then doing synthetic generation from it.  This again, I suspect is the fuzzification and De-Fuzzification of understanding of the text, it is the same as generative AI.  I think the problem of maintaining entropy is overcome by Fuzzy C means clustering and/or K-means clustering.  K-means originated from improvements in communication systems and uses a pseudo random initialization.
> 
> Great talk, and very interesting, thank you for sharing!

> Andrej Karpathy’s Vision: The Future of Education (Timestamp 01:57:08+)
> 
> Personalized, Tutor-Like Learning:
> Karpathy believes the optimal education experience is deeply personalized, like having an elite, real human tutor. In his Korean learning journey, a one-on-one tutor quickly diagnosed his level and delivered just-right challenges, which no current AI (not even top LLMs) can truly do yet. Real progress will enable everyone to access such tailored, adaptive learning—the system understands you, probes your knowledge gaps, scaffolds difficult material, and keeps you always challenged but not overwhelmed or bored.
> 
> Technical Ramps to Knowledge:
> Great teaching builds ramps to knowledge—carefully sequenced material where each concept builds directly on the last, with minimal “dependency tangles.” Karpathy emphasizes the need to maximize “eurekas per second”—flashes of understanding—by untangling knowledge so students never get stuck, always progressing at their own optimal rate. He sees this structural challenge as a deeply technical problem, on par with AI research itself.
> 
> AI in Education: Current and Future:
> Today’s LLMs (like ChatGPT) are useful for conventional studying, making content, and answering questions, but fall short at being true tutors or curriculum designers. They excel at boilerplate tasks, basic Q&A, and autocomplete, but lack deep cognitive adaptation and judgment. The real future lies in fusing human educators (who design the technical “ramp”) with increasingly capable AI assistants and automated TAs.
> 
> Eureka/Education Startup:
> Instead of joining an AI lab, Karpathy is building a modern, elite educational institution (nicknamed “Starfleet Academy”) focused on technical mastery and deep learning, starting with AI and coding. He’s building both physical and digital offerings—first, a flagship course (LLM101N); eventually, a scalable educational system where the best experts “codify” their expertise for mass audiences, assisted by AI.
> 
> Automation’s Impact on Motivation:
> Pre-AGI, people learn primarily to improve careers—education is pragmatic. Post-AGI, when everything is automated, education becomes a form of fun, self-improvement, health—like going to the gym even when machines can do all the lifting. Humans will learn languages, advanced curricula, and many subjects just for enjoyment and flourishing.
> 
> Human Empowerment vs. Disempowerment:
> Karpathy’s biggest worry is a “WALL-E or Idiocracy” scenario where humanity is sidelined by automation. Empowerment and growth must remain possible—education should enable cognitive flourishing and keep humans “in the loop,” so that technological progress doesn’t leave us behind.
> 
> Practical Advice for Educators and Learners:
> 
> Build ramps: Sequence material for clear progression and understanding.
> 
> Don’t just memorize—build things from scratch, explain things to others, manipulate the material for true mastery.
> 
> Great teachers motivate by exposing pain points before giving solutions.
> 
> Learning should be calibrated—never too hard or trivial.
> 
> Use collaboration, self-explanation, and active recall; motivation is technical and can be “engineered” by better educational structures.
> 
> Key takeaways:
> 
> The future is AI-powered, personalized, always-adaptive education.
> 
> Human educators remain central, codifying their wisdom; AI assists and eventually evolves toward true tutoring.
> 
> Learning will be both empowering and enjoyable—necessary for work before AGI, but fun and self-driven after full automation.
> 
> Maximizing understanding and motivation is a solvable technical problem and the core mission for education in an AI-dominated future.

> Current LLMs generate answers by averaging probable patterns, not by testing them. Almost 100 years ago, philosopher Karl Popper showed that inference/inductive logic—the same logic underlying LLM responses—fails without a “falsification” step that tests scientific theories. Adding such an architectural layer would enable models to actively challenge and reject errors, turning probabilistic guesses (think Nassim Taleb’s turkey problem) into far more reliable outputs. This would attract high-consequence users—paying customers—who can’t afford mistakes. Frankly, LLM developers can’t afford NOT to build this layer.

### Comment 1370
- comment_id: UgzMJ4TJgZJy1x-w2D54AaABAg.AOOzZePrJ4wAOQUPCkjAYa
- parent_id: UgzMJ4TJgZJy1x-w2D54AaABAg
- author: @Jackson_Zheng
- author_id: UC_KvUnSN4Q41Uf-o8lj_bTw
- published_at: 2025-11-19T00:00:00.000Z
- like_count: 0
- is_favorited: false
- author_is_uploader: false

> You really don't need personalisation. Traditional education is bad not because it lacks personalisation but because it's not giving the context before the explanation.
> Stories are the perfect example that shows why you don't need any personalisation to be interested. A well written story has inherent structure that's positioned to captivate the reader's attention no matter who they are.
> It starts with a character going along with their usual routine -> then there's an inciting incident that breaks routine -> high stakes are presented as motivation for the character to take action -> character deliberates on what actions to take -> we see the result of that decision play out in real time -> the character then adjusts their choice based on the outcome/new information -> and so on and so forth.
> 
> All the information is given right there and regardless of your background or personal understanding, you can still follow along because it's using the right structure to deliver the information.
> There is no incentives in schools to do that as they are teaching to a test and aren't required to get the attention of kids.
> This is why educational material is so much better on the internet than in schools because YouTubers and content creators are directly incentivised to capture attention and hold it while delivering the information.
> 
> 
> Most of the issues with schools can be solved just by having the teachers be trained on effective teaching methods, rather than teaching the teachers the course material they need to teach (which is what happens most of the time). So what ends up happening is that teachers have to learn the art of teaching for themselves and that just leads to a lot of bad teachers who are there just to get the paycheck at the end of every month.

### Comment 1392
- comment_id: UgzapW403nM1A6kBINV4AaABAg.AOOvP3riBqmAOQVto10QwH

- like_count: 2

> If you're talking about evolution of a brain-like learning architecture, essentially building a baby, then I think the problem is than you'd first need to decide what are all the piece parts whose organization/assembly you are going to try to evolve. It doesn't seem computationally feasible to just evolve arbitrary neural networks comprised of trillions of neurons - you need to narrow the problem into a much fewer number of assemblies/functional blocks.
> 
> I think if someone knew the right pieces then there would be no need for an automated evolutionary process, since it would imply you'd already understood the problem well enough and how these piece parts might/should interact, that you could hand design the initial overall architecture, and then iterate from there.
> 
> I'm not sure that we don't already know roughly what it would take to build a brain, but it's just that some parts of it like continual embodied learning, are difficult. Researchers have been trying a long time to come up with an alternative to gradient descent, without much success. It's one thing to say that brains learn by Hebbian fire-together, wire-together, or STDP, but another to actually convert that into a large scale successful prototype.

> @benbridgwater6479  Thanks for the reply! I'm sure the following is mostly useless thinking, but anyway here it is: 
> 
> Have we really explored all possibilities for continued embodied learning? I guess it sort of seems to me like it shouldn't be that hard to build something that works off of electricity or biology that has some fundamental access to some resources and it could change it's structure if it could figure out how. So you give this very basic system some set of beginner, very basic goals, that once solved would be the absolute bare bones of being able to store information to solve the problem next time, you'd probably need the system to be able to do a couple other MVPs of some of the overall functionalities of... essentially the brain. Once it's able to do that, then continuing to guide it through a goal process where it's able to eventually solve complex problems having essentially built itself. 
> I'm not saying this is a new question by any means, but a question that does come to mind for me is, If you know the approximate goals of what the system needs to be able to do, why can't we build a simple system to do that? And I guess we have, but we haven't built a system that can truly learn basic things and embody them and change it's own architecture to be able to solve the next problem. We have some basic machine learning algorithms, but I don't think they've solved the problem in an embodied sense.
> It just seems like if you were able to build some very miniscule starting point of it being able to evolve itself. Then basically you could just take it down a simple evolutionary process of: hey, solve this problem, you know, create multiple copies, whichever one survives will go on... like stuff like that, and eventually you would get to the same level of intelligence as humans possibly.
> I know I'm no expert in this, I just am thinking about it and it's hard to explain some of this stuff, but just wanted to write it here anyway.

> For partial solution evaluation we use sense of beauty.  
> We sense beauty with
> 1. symmetry 
> 2. simplicity (compression, Occam's razor)
> 3. completion 
> 
> So, there are basic, fundamental, built in judges that we have that help navigate through solution. 
> 
> Over time, this judge also acquires knowledge, so we increase reward for resemblance. If during solving a problem it starts to appear like something we've seen before than we assign a higher reward to that. 
> 
> And finally there is a land of tasks where you could sanity check all the steps along the way against the ground truth (logical contradictions, laws of physics, simple facts like Paris is capital of France).

### Comment 1428
- comment_id: UgzfwQmXsN4UkgjkSL14AaABAg.AOOpTan__YQAOSzF8AVZ61

- like_count: 0
- is_favorited: false

> I don't think beauty/simplicity can be taken as a proxy for correctness. Those are more a matter of human preference, and perhaps given multiple solutions to a problem one should prefer the simpler and more profound one.
> 
> Sanity/fact checking of individual solution steps, while necessary, doesn't mean that this was a good choice of next step and will lead to a solution.
> 
> The real way to evaluate progress towards a goal is to have had a high level plan to begin with, essentially a series of subgoals, where you've established ahead of time that if you can achieve these subgoals then you will have solved the problem. Of course this isn't how an LLM is always going to work, unless specifically prompted to do so, but there have been some recent papers about using this sort of plan-then-execute type of approach.
> 
> However, it's not obvious that using process-based RL is the best way to encourage this sort of reasoning, since it's not about individual reasoning steps being correct in isolation, but rather about them working towards the plan that was established up front. Maybe a better way would be to generate a synthetic dataset of problem solving that used this plan then execute approach,, then just fine tune on that?

> Regarding the suggestion that humans might lose “control” to AI -
> 
> I’d argue that the entire notion of control, as it’s commonly used, is incoherent once you examine how the universe actually operates. Nothing truly controls anything else, because every process, every decision, every action arises from prior causes that extend beyond the system we’re looking at. Everything behaves according to the laws of physics, and every system has inputs from outside itself that determine its outputs.
> 
> Humans create the illusion of control by drawing arbitrary boundaries around complex interactions. We say “this person decided” or “this system acted,” but those are just convenient fictions for describing a tangled web of influences. In reality, there are no clean boundaries - only continuous chains of causation stretching outward indefinitely.
> 
> The human mind is not the origin of any chain of events. It’s a transient node within a vast network of interactions including genetic, environmental, and physical - all shaping its states moment to moment. The mind doesn’t choose how it is influenced by stimuli, and thus cannot truly control its own outputs.
> 
> As a simple thought experiment: try to explain how a thought appears in your consciousness. Can you predict or produce the next one at will? Most of us can’t. Thoughts just arrive. We do not experience selecting them from a list of all possible thoughts. If we cannot even control the arising of our own thoughts, then what sense does it make to claim we control the actions that follow from them?
> 
> Control, then, is not a feature of reality - it’s a framing convenience. A linguistic shortcut that lets us navigate an incomprehensibly interdependent universe by pretending that boundaries and autonomy exist where they do not.

> I would argue that effective action selection is the basis of reasoning, which is really nothing more than chained what-if action (cf reasoning step) outcome predictions.

> Sparks a thought, when i was coming up, nobody was confused about AI- it meant a fully composed general intelligence capable of original, creative thinking and to whatever extent permitted, volition. Watched marketeers jump in over and over and over again to try to make various kinds of automation into "AI" over the last 30 years. Now we have machine learning platforms (LLMs etc) that can badly, but consistently mimic (but never create), natural human communication, and the marketing nonsense finally stuck the landing. Everything is "AI" and nothing is automation, machine learning, robots (what we're actually using) or anything else with a useful descriptive denominator; And yet, we have only incrementally further along in the original goal of what we might now call "Classical AI", or what we started with in the first place. Karpathy is having nearly the same conversation I heard when introduced to AI decades ago

> AI was always an umbrella term.  There never was a clear line between "true" and untrue(?) AI.  I always thought the term was deliberately meant to be vague or all-inclusive because we neither wanted nor were in a position to draw limits around the field.  At the first AI conference there was a geometry theorem prover and Solomonoff's talk on a universal inference algorithm (depth-first search on all Turing machine programs). The old timers would have been just as surprised by LLMs as our contemporaries because it's genuinely significant stuff coming together from some surprising quarters.  And yes AI people were thinking of free will and creativity, as well as humor and emotion, trying to scope out the whole system, along with less far-off targets.

> He's 100% right about distilling the cognitive core of LLM's by way of squeezing out hard knowledge from the weights. A big reason why I'm bearish on hyperscaling is that I think there's a ton of overhead in current models that can be unlocked by decoupling fact retrieval and cognition. ### Comment 1874
- comment_id: UgzP1kGc3fiYRNX63qF4AaABAg.AOOJspPTzNGAOQh74nbGFx
- parent_id: UgzP1kGc3fiYRNX63qF4AaABAg

- like_count: 1

> It's interesting why current LLM training sets include so much utter garbage, a fact that Andrej referred to more than once. Would it not be better to filter out the garbage (would need to be automated), and strive for a more curated training set of useful, factually correct and reasoning-rich data? 
> 
> OTOH, I'm not convinced that it's even conceptually possible to separate knowledge and reasoning. The core generic mechanics of reasoning are simple enough - basically multi-step what-if prediction, including backtracking and impasse resolution. However when it comes to actual reasoning, then you need more than just the mechanics, you need the relevant declarative, procedural, and episodic (personal experience) knowledge for that specific domain. Analogies aside, being able to reason about fixing your car engine isn't going to help you reason about how to code NanoChat.
> 
> Of course some reasoning generalizes pretty well, so if you're a trained mechanic working on a new car model you've never seen before, then probably the manual tells you 90% of what you need to know (with the other 10% being the school of hard knocks stuff they omitted), but still retrieval is no substitute for experience.
